title: Third difference: act-deformity—three scholastic venial species excused before a gracious Judge
source_text: XLII. Tertio dicit peccatum mortale & veniale differre ratione ipsorum actuum; quoniam foeditas, sive deformitas, quae in peccatis venialibus invenitur, multo minor est ea quae peccatis mortalibus inest: propterea quod in omni peccato veniali est ali-quid quod offensam per illud commissam attenuat, & apud gratiosum judicem quodam-modo excusat. Quod postea probat percurrens tres illas peccati venialis species, quae a Scholasticis distingui solent. Nam earum primam, hoc est, peccatum veniale ex genere suo, apud Deum gratiose, & secundum multitudinem miserationum suarum judicantem, excusat, ut ait, offensae levitas (comparativa scilicet, cum nullum pec-catum absolute sit leve) quam habet ex ipsa natura specifica actus in se considerati, absque respectu ad modum agendi, aut ad particularem materiam in qua committitur. Ut patet, verbi causa, in verbo otioso, in risu nimio, &c. Secundam vero peccati venialis speciem, hoc est, peccatum ex subreptione, excusat levitas offensae quam habet, non ex natura specifica actus in se considerati, sed ex modo quo actus ille ab agente procedit; quia videlicet, agens non plene & sufficienter deliberavit: ut, ex-empli gratia, in subito appetitu vindictae, aut libidinis. Quoniam appetitus vindictae, ex natura sua specifica, non est peccatum leve; sed per accidens est leve, quia fit ex indeliberatione. Tertiam vero speciem, hoc est, peccatum veniale ex parvitate materiae, excusat levitas offensae quam habet, non ex propria natura talis actus, sed ex limitatione ejus ad particularem materiam; ut in furto unius oboli. Nam furtum ex natura sua specifica non est peccatum leve, sed ex accidente; quia committitur in re minoris mo-menti.
pass_a_gloss: Thirdly he says mortal and venial sin differ by reason of the acts themselves; because the foulness or deformity found in venial sins is much less than that which is in mortal sins: for in every venial sin there is something that attenuates the offense committed by it and somehow excuses it before a gracious Judge. Which he afterwards proves by running through those three species of venial sin which the Scholastics are wont to distinguish. For the first of them—that is, venial sin from its own genus—before God judging graciously and according to the multitude of his mercies, the lightness of the offense excuses (comparative lightness, of course, since no sin is absolutely light), which it has from the specific nature of the act considered in itself, without respect to the manner of acting or to the particular matter in which it is committed. As appears, for example, in an idle word, in excessive laughter, etc. But the second species of venial sin—that is, sin from surprise—the lightness of offense excuses which it has not from the specific nature of the act considered in itself, but from the manner in which that act proceeds from the agent; because namely the agent did not fully and sufficiently deliberate: as, for example, in a sudden appetite of revenge or of lust. Since the appetite of revenge from its specific nature is not a light sin; but it is light by accident, because it arises from lack of deliberation. But the third species—that is, venial sin from smallness of matter—the lightness of offense excuses which it has not from the proper nature of such an act, but from its limitation to a particular matter; as in the theft of one obol. For theft from its specific nature is not a light sin, but by accident; because it is committed in a matter of lesser moment.
pass_b_english: Venial acts carry less deformity: something softens the offense before a gracious Judge.
Baron tracks the three scholastic species—by genus, by surprise, by small matter—each ‘light’ only comparatively or by accident.

choices.why: No sin absolutely light; lightness is relative before mercy.
